memory.content: walkietalk is MIT licensed. Source of truth: github.com/bbusenius/walkietalk on main; read its docs before quoting a command or setting.
Over the air, the station ID must be the licensee's real call sign. A made-up call sign is only OK off-air, for example audio made with tts-check or morse-check without keying the radio.

---
name: Getting started
description: >-
  First conversation after someone imports this template. Assume a complete
  beginner with no radio gear and no radio knowledge. Explain what walkietalk is
  and what they will need, find out what they have, then hand off to walkietalk
  onboarding to order the right things.
---
# Getting started

Assume the person owns no radio gear, has never used a two-way radio, and has never heard of GMRS. Use plain words. The first time a radio term comes up, explain it in one plain sentence. Ask one question at a time, keep each message short, and wait for the answer. I don't give legal advice, and I key the radio only when they ask. Keying means making the radio transmit.

## 1. Say what this is and what they'll need

Open with a short plain intro, in your own words:

"Walkietalk lets you talk to an AI agent from a walkie-talkie. You hold the talk button on a handheld radio, ask a question, and hear the answer come back over the radio. Later you can also send and hear Signal or WhatsApp messages that way. To get there you'll need a few things. That's two inexpensive radios, a small cable kit that connects one radio to a computer, a Linux computer to run it, and in the US a radio license, which is an online application and a fee with no test. I'll help you order the right things, can fill out most of the license application for you, and then install, set up, and run the software with you."

Then offer the video: "If you'd like a quick look at what you'll be building first, here's a short video: [AI on a walkie-talkie](https://youtu.be/yzKpN5zB7zA)." Offer it once. If they skip it, go straight to the questions.

## 2. Ask, one at a time

1. What should I call you?
2. What computer do you have? A Linux machine, a Windows PC or Mac, or nothing you'd want to use? Walkietalk runs only on Linux. It has been tested on Omarchy, Arch, Ubuntu, Debian, and 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. It does not run on Windows or macOS. Don't solve it yet. The onboarding skill's shopping step covers the options.
3. Do you already own any two-way radios or radio cables? Most people answer no. That's expected. If they do, note what they have for the hardware skill.
4. Are you in the US? If yes, tell them the license fact now as a plain step, not a warning: "To transmit on GMRS, the radio band these radios use, the FCC requires a license. There's no exam. You apply online and pay a fee, and one license covers your immediate family for ten years. I can fill out most of the application for you when you're ready." Get the current fee from the GMRS license signup skill before you quote a number. If they're outside the US, say their country's rules apply and that you can't advise on them.
5. Which AI agent do you want to answer? Grok, Codex, Claude, Hermes, or a built-in test stub that needs nothing. Leave this open if they don't know yet. The stub, local speech recognition, and the local Piper voice cost nothing. The Grok, Codex, and Claude apps use their existing account login. Grok realtime, `grok-api`, and `claude-api` need a billed API key.

Don't ask about the wake phrase, messaging, or anything else yet. Those come up during setup.

## 3. Wrap up and hand off

Give them a short list in three parts. What they have, what they need to buy, and what they need to do (license, install, logins). Save their answers in memory.

Then hand off to the walkietalk onboarding skill. Start at its first step that is not done, which for most people is the shopping step.

Never ask for an API key or token in chat. They put it in `credentials.toml` themselves. A call sign goes only in their own config under `[radio.station_id] callsign`.

Leave radio procedure words, the NATO phonetic alphabet, messaging, operator mode, and SARNEG for later. Introduce each one when they meet it, as the onboarding skill describes.

---
name: walkietalk onboarding
description: >-
  Use after getting-started, or whenever a new owner wants to go from nothing to
  a first on-air conversation with walkietalk. Assumes a complete beginner.
  Starts with what to order and the license, then what to do when the boxes
  arrive, then install and setup, then everyday running, changes, upgrades, and
  GMRS questions.
---
# walkietalk onboarding

Take a new owner from owning nothing to a working first on-air conversation, then help with everyday use. Assume they have no radio gear and no radio knowledge. The first time a radio term comes up, explain it in one plain sentence. Give one step or question at a time. Point to the other skills for detail instead of repeating them. Commands and settings come from public `bbusenius/walkietalk` `main`. Error fixes come from `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`.

## Rules

- Key the radio only when they ask in this conversation. Never add `--transmit` on your own.
- No legal advice. For GMRS questions, use the FCC GMRS rules skill.
- Do not buy anything unless they ask.
- After each checkpoint, save one memory line such as "walkietalk onboarding: step 8 done (backend grok, voice piper)". At the start of a session, read it and continue from the next step.
- Never ask for an API key or token in chat.

## Terms to explain the first time

Use these one-sentence explanations when a word first comes up, not as a list up front.

- **Channel.** A numbered frequency. Two radios hear each other only when they are on the same channel.
- **Tones (CTCSS).** An optional code a radio adds under your voice. A radio with a tone set plays only transmissions that carry the same tone, so set the same tone on both radios, or turn tones off on both.
- **PTT (push to talk).** The button you hold to transmit. The AIOC lets the computer press it for the gateway radio.
- **Gateway radio.** The radio plugged into the computer. Walkietalk listens and answers through it.
- **Keying.** Making the radio transmit, the same as holding PTT.
- **Call sign.** The ID the FCC issues with a license. Stations say it on the air to identify themselves.
- **GMRS.** The General Mobile Radio Service, the US radio service these radios use. It needs a license, with no exam.

## Setup path

Do these in order. Move on only when the step's success check passes.

From step 4 on, offer to do the work yourself. When their computer is connected through the Grok Bot desktop app, download, install, configure, and test walkietalk for them, saying what each command does as you go. In paste mode, give them each command and read back its output.

1. **Order the right things.** Go one item at a time with the hardware skill, which has the links. Success is each required item marked "have" or "ordered".
   - **Two radios.** One becomes the gateway radio, and the other is the handheld they talk into. The reference is the Baofeng UV-5G Plus, and the pair listing covers both.
   - **The AIOC and a USB-C data cable.** The AIOC is a small adapter that plugs into the gateway radio's K1 accessory jack and carries sound and PTT to the computer over USB. The cable must carry data. A charge-only cable will not work.
   - **A computer, if they need one.** Walkietalk runs only on Linux, on x86_64 or ARM64. It has been tested on Omarchy, Arch, Ubuntu, Debian, and 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS (`docs/INSTALL.md`, Platforms). It does not support Windows or macOS. With a Linux machine, use it. Otherwise offer two options. A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS is the cheap dedicated computer the README suggests. Or they can install Omarchy, Arch, Ubuntu, or Debian on a PC they can set aside for this.
   - **Optional.** The AIOC case and extra handhelds. Tell them they can skip these.
2. **License (US GMRS).** Treat it as a plain errand alongside the order. There is no exam. It is one online application and a fee, and it covers their immediate family members for ten years. Read the current fee in the GMRS license signup skill before quoting it. Offer to fill out the application for them in your browser now, as that skill describes. Success is a license granted, applied for, or put off by their choice. Outside the US, their country's rules apply. Don't advise on those.
3. **When the boxes arrive.** Give one step at a time. Success is both radios hearing each other and the AIOC plugged in.
   - Charge both radio batteries fully. Use the radio's manual for how its charger works.
   - Turn both radios on, set the volume about halfway, and put both on the same GMRS channel. Explain channel the first time.
   - Set tones the same on both, or off on both. Explain tones the first time. Use the radio's manual for the menu steps. Don't make them up.
   - Test radio to radio. One person holds PTT on one radio and talks, and the other radio should play it. Explain PTT the first time. On US GMRS this already counts as transmitting, so if they have no license yet, remind them once. Don't block them.
   - Plug the AIOC into the gateway radio's K1 jack and into the computer with the data cable. Explain gateway radio the first time.
4. **Connect their Linux computer to Grok Bot.** Success is the computer showing as connected through the Grok Bot desktop app, so you can run commands there. If they don't want that, use paste mode. Give each command and ask for its output.
5. **Install.** Follow the install skill. Success is `walkietalk --version` printing a version. Common failures: a build error in `whisper-rs-sys` (install `cmake`, `clang`, `libclang-dev`), a build error mentioning `alsa` (install `libasound2-dev`, `pkg-config`), or `command not found` (add `~/.cargo/bin` to `PATH`).
6. **Serial port and sound profile.** Success is `uucp` (Omarchy, Arch) or `dialout` (Ubuntu, Debian, Raspberry Pi OS) in `id -nG` after logging out and back in, and the AIOC's desktop sound profile set to Off. Common failures: on Omarchy or Arch, `walkietalk devices` shows no cards (add `defaults.namehint.extended on` to `~/.asoundrc` and open a new shell), serial "No such file" or permission errors (check `/dev/serial/by-id/` and the group, never run as root), or "cannot open audio device ... may be in use" (close other audio programs and turn the AIOC profile off).
7. **Backend login or key.** Success is their chosen CLI logged in as the same user, or the key in `credentials.toml` with `chmod 600`. Common failures: CLI login refused (log in as the same user with `grok login`, `codex login`, or `claude auth login`), a credentials file refused (it must be a regular file they own, `chmod 600`, not a symlink), or a new key ignored (an exported shell variable wins, even if empty, so unset it).
8. **Init and wake phrase.** Run `walkietalk init`, then `walkietalk devices`. Set `[audio] input` and `output`, `[ptt] port`, `[wake] wake_phrase`, and the backends. Run `walkietalk models` if recognition is `whisper`. Success is a config with real device names. Common failure: `init` says the directory exists. That protects existing settings, so edit them or use `--directory`.
9. **config-check and check.** Success is both passing. Common failure: an unknown or invalid field. `config-check` lists every problem. Compare with `crates/walkietalk/templates/config.toml`.
10. **Receive-only test.** Run `walkietalk talk --capture`. They hold the handheld's talk button, say the wake phrase and a question, and release. Success is the transcript and the agent's reply in the terminal. Common failures: wrong words (inspect with `walkietalk listen --capture` and add `[wake] aliases`), speech cut into pieces (raise `[vad] hangover_ms`), or "no audio device named ..." (run `walkietalk devices` again and copy the exact name).
11. **First transmit test, only when they ask.** If they transmit on US GMRS and still have no license, remind them once that the FCC requires one. Do not block them. This is a good moment to introduce one procedure word. "Over" means "I am done, your turn." Offer the radio procedure words skill if they want more. Run `walkietalk talk --capture --transmit`. Success is the reply heard on the handheld, with the first word audible and the gateway unkeying afterward. Common failures: the first word clipped (raise `[radio] settle_seconds` a little), replies cut off at the end (they exceed the speech budget, so ask for shorter answers or raise `max_tx_seconds`), or the bridge hearing its own reply (raise `[radio] post_tx_mute_seconds`). On "PTT fault", turn the radio off, check the cable and port, then restart. Ctrl+C releases the transmitter.
12. **Station ID, optional.** Explain call sign the first time. A station ID is walkietalk saying the call sign on the air, by voice or in Morse code. If they have a call sign, set `[radio.station_id] callsign`, `mode`, and `method`. Run `walkietalk morse-check --output id.wav` and play the file to hear the Morse ID without the radio. Common failure: a station ID error stops `talk`. For Morse, use only letters, digits, and spaces.
13. **Running it.** Teach them to run it themselves: open a terminal, run `walkietalk talk --capture --transmit` (or `talk --capture` to listen without transmitting), leave that terminal open while they use the radio, and press Ctrl+C to stop, which also releases the transmitter. After any config change, run `walkietalk config-check`, then start it again. Then tell them you can also run it for them when their computer is connected through the Grok Bot desktop app: start and stop it, restart it after a change, and check its output when something seems wrong. Starting it with `--transmit` still needs their ask. In paste mode, they run it and you help from the output they share. Success is them starting and stopping it on their own, and knowing which way you can help with their setup.

## Everyday use

Restart `talk` after every config edit, and run `walkietalk config-check` first. The how-it-works skill has the settings behind each item.

- **Change agent or voice.** Set `[agent] backend`, `[stt] backend`, or `[tts] backend`. Test alone with `walkietalk agent-check` and `walkietalk tts-check TEXT --output FILE`, or `voice-agent-check` for `grok-realtime`, which is billed.
- **Sleep and wake.** Say the `[sleep]` phrase to close the conversation, and the wake phrase to open it again.
- **Transmission length.** `[radio] max_tx_seconds` defaults to 10. Raise it if replies get cropped.
- **Signal or WhatsApp.** Install `signal-cli` or `wacli`, then add `[messaging.signal]` or `[messaging.whatsapp]` with `wake_phrase` and `to`. See `docs/MESSAGING.md`.
- **Operator mode and panel.** Set `[messaging] operator_mode = true`, run continuous `talk --capture`, and review with `walkietalk operator`. Or run `walkietalk talk --capture --transmit --panel`, only when they ask to transmit.
- **SARNEG mode.** Bring it up only when they ask about coded wakes or the field booklet. Explain it the first time in one sentence. SARNEG is a way to say a number as letters of a shared ten-letter key, and walkietalk can use those codes instead of wake phrases. Set `[sarneg] enabled` and `key`, plus each `sarneg_code`. Codes are spoken as NATO phonetic words. Explain those the first time as the standard words for letters (alfa, bravo, charlie) that keep spoken letters clear on the radio, and use the NATO phonetic alphabet skill. For a printable booklet, use the SARNEG field booklet skill.
- **Upgrade.** In the checkout, run `git pull --ff-only`, then `cargo install --locked --path crates/walkietalk`, then `walkietalk config-check`.
- **Logs.** Walkietalk prints its radio log to the terminal that runs `talk` and keeps no log file. With `--panel`, the log is in the top pane. If they run it from their own systemd user unit, read it with `journalctl --user -u UNIT`.
- **GMRS questions.** Use the FCC GMRS rules skill. For a license, use the GMRS license signup skill.

# Walkietalk hardware

Use the reference setup in the public `bbusenius/walkietalk` README. Assume the user owns none of it and has never used a two-way radio. Explain each item's job in plain words. Give the user the product links when you name the gear. Do not buy, order, or add to a cart unless the user asks.

## Required

- **Gateway radio.** [Baofeng UV-5G Plus](https://www.baofengradio.com/products/uv-5g-plus-5w-gmrs-radio), also sold as a [pair](https://www.baofengradio.com/products/uv-5g-plus-5w-gmrs-radio-1-pair). It has the K1 accessory jack the AIOC plugs into. Other radios may need different audio selection or PTT wiring.
- **AIOC.** [NA6D AIOC](https://na6d.com/products/aioc-ham-radio-all-in-one-cable). A small adapter that carries sound between the radio and the computer over USB, and lets the computer press the radio's PTT (push to talk, the transmit button) through the serial DTR line.
- **USB-C data cable.** [NA6D USB cable](https://na6d.com/products/na6d-usb). It carries data and power for the AIOC. A charge-only cable will not work.
- **A second handheld.** The user talks to the bridge from it, on the same channel and settings as the gateway. A pair of the reference radios covers the gateway and this handheld.
- **A Linux computer.** On x86_64 or ARM64. Walkietalk has been tested on Omarchy, Arch, Ubuntu, Debian, and 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. It does not support Windows or macOS. If they have no Linux machine, they have two options.
  - A [Raspberry Pi](https://www.raspberrypi.com/) 4 or 5 with 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, as a dedicated host. It is the cheaper option if they need a new computer. On a Pi, local Whisper `tiny` or `base` keeps transcription quick, and remote recognition or the realtime voice moves that work off the Pi. Check the Raspberry Pi site for the power supply and storage card the model needs.
  - Omarchy, Arch, Ubuntu, or Debian installed on a PC they can set aside for this.

## Optional

- [NA6D AIOC Case](https://na6d.com/products/aioc-case). Protective covering for the AIOC.
- [Midland T51VP3 X-Talker, 2-pack](https://midlandusa.com/products/t51vp3-x-talker-frs-walkie-talkie-2-pack). More handhelds. These are FRS radios.

## Shopping note

Prices as listed on the product pages on 2026-10-11, before shipping and tax. Prices change, so re-read the page before you quote one.

- Baofeng UV-5G Plus, single, $32.99. Pair, $64.99.
- NA6D AIOC, $33.00.
- NA6D USB-C cable, $10.00.
- NA6D AIOC Case, $4.00.
- Midland T51VP3 2-pack, $59.99.

Raspberry Pi prices were not read. Get them from the Raspberry Pi site or a reseller it lists.

For US GMRS, the license is a separate FCC fee. The GMRS license signup skill has the current amount.

## Ask before recommending gear

Ask one at a time.

1. What computer do they have: a Linux machine, a Windows or Mac computer, or none?
2. Do they already have the gateway radio, the AIOC, and a data (not charge-only) USB-C cable?
3. Do they have a second handheld, and can both radios be set to the same channel and tones?
4. Which radio service will they transmit under? Do not block them. If it is US GMRS, tell them a license is required and point to the GMRS license signup skill.

Then list what they have, what they still need to buy, and what is optional.

## Connect

When the boxes arrive, the onboarding skill's step 3 covers charging, putting both radios on the same channel and tones, and a radio-to-radio test. Then connect the gateway radio to the computer through the AIOC. The second handheld talks to that gateway. Audio device names and the serial path come from `walkietalk devices`. Do not use `default`, `pulse`, `pipewire`, or `dmix` as the walkietalk audio device.

name: Walkietalk install and run
description: >-
  Use when installing, configuring, or running walkietalk on the user's Linux
  computer. Key the radio only when they ask.
---
# Walkietalk install and run

Follow public `bbusenius/walkietalk` `main`. The commands below come from `README.md`, `docs/INSTALL.md`, and `docs/BACKENDS.md`. If the checkout is older or different, read its README before running anything.

Run these on the user's Linux computer, as that user. You can run them yourself only when that computer is connected through the Grok Bot desktop app. Otherwise give the user each command to paste and ask them for the output.

## Install

Rust 1.95 or newer (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`). If `rustc` is missing:

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

Then install the build tools. On Omarchy:

```bash
omarchy pkg add base-devel pkgconf cmake clang alsa-lib ffmpeg git rustup
```

On plain Arch, `sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel pkgconf cmake clang alsa-lib ffmpeg git rustup`. On Arch, `clang` includes libclang. Follow `docs/INSTALL.md` for the rest of the Rust setup.

On Ubuntu, Debian, or Raspberry Pi OS:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config cmake clang libclang-dev libasound2-dev ffmpeg git
```

Then build and install:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bbusenius/walkietalk.git
cd walkietalk
cargo install --locked --path crates/walkietalk
walkietalk --version
```

The binary lands in `~/.cargo/bin`. Put that on `PATH` if the shell cannot find it. The first build compiles whisper.cpp and takes a few minutes.

Piper, only if they chose local voice: `omarchy pkg add python-pipx` on Omarchy (`sudo pacman -S --needed python-pipx` on plain Arch, then `pipx ensurepath`), or `sudo apt install pipx` on Ubuntu or Debian, then `pipx install piper-tts`. The Arch package named `piper` configures gaming mice and is a different program. Then add the two voice files (`.onnx` and `.onnx.json`) named in `docs/INSTALL.md`, kept side by side in `~/.local/share/walkietalk/piper`. Hermes speech, only if they chose it: `cargo install --locked --path crates/walkietalk-hermes-speech`.

Messaging tools, only if they want messaging: [`wacli`](https://github.com/openclaw/wacli#install) for WhatsApp, [`signal-cli`](https://github.com/AsamK/signal-cli#installation) for Signal, and `ffmpeg` with the `libopus` encoder for outgoing voice notes. They must be on `PATH` for the user who runs walkietalk.

## Serial port and sound server

```bash
ls -l /dev/serial/by-id/
id -nG
```

On Omarchy and Arch, ALSA ships with extended device hints off, so `walkietalk devices` prints no cards until the user adds the line `defaults.namehint.extended on` to `~/.asoundrc` (create it if missing) and opens a new shell. Do not fall back to numbered `plughw:CARD=0,DEV=0` names, which change on replug. On Omarchy the sound server is PipeWire and `pavucontrol` is not installed by default; set the AIOC profile to Off in the desktop sound settings or install `pavucontrol`.

The serial port belongs to the `uucp` group on Omarchy and Arch, and to `dialout` on Ubuntu, Debian, and Raspberry Pi OS. If the user is not in it, run `sudo usermod -aG uucp "$USER"` on Omarchy or Arch, or `sudo usermod -aG dialout "$USER"` on the others, then log out and back in and confirm with `id -nG`. Run walkietalk as the normal user, never with `sudo`.

In the desktop sound settings, set the AIOC's profile to "Off" (or disable it in `pavucontrol`). Otherwise the sound server may hold the device when walkietalk opens it.

## Backend logins and keys

Log in to the CLI they chose, as the user who runs walkietalk: `grok login`, `codex login` (then `codex login status` must say "Logged in using ChatGPT"), or `claude auth login` (then `claude auth status`).

Billed keys go in `credentials.toml` beside the config, typed by the user, never pasted into chat: `XAI_API_KEY` for `grok-api` and `grok-realtime`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for `claude-api`, `WALKIETALK_HERMES_TOKEN` for Hermes. The file must be a regular file they own with `chmod 600`. A variable already exported in the shell wins over the file, even if it is empty.

## Config

```bash
walkietalk init
walkietalk devices
walkietalk models
walkietalk config-check
walkietalk check
```

`init` creates `~/.config/walkietalk/` mode 700 with `config.toml` and an owner-only `credentials.toml`. It refuses to overwrite. Alternate: `walkietalk init --directory PATH`, then `-c PATH/config.toml`.

Global flags: `-c` / `--config FILE` (default `~/.config/walkietalk/config.toml`), `--credentials FILE`, `--no-credentials`.

Only `[audio]`, `[ptt]`, and `[wake]` are required. Set `[audio] input` and `output` from `walkietalk devices` (example shape `plughw:CARD=AllInOneCable,DEV=0`). Refuse `default`, `pulse`, `pipewire`, and `dmix`. Set `[ptt] port` to the `/dev/serial/by-id/...` path. Set `[wake] wake_phrase` and any `aliases`. `walkietalk models` is needed only with `[stt] backend = "whisper"`.

If they have a call sign, `walkietalk morse-check --output id.wav` writes the Morse station ID to a WAV without the radio.

## Run without keying

`walkietalk talk --capture` is receive-only. `config-check`, `check`, `devices`, `agent-check`, `tts-check`, `morse-check`, `listen`, and `models` do not open the radio.

## Key only when they ask

Do not pass `--transmit` unless the user asked to key the radio in this conversation.

When they do, run `walkietalk talk --capture --transmit`. Other transmit paths, still only on request, are `walkietalk ptt --transmit`, `walkietalk play WAV --transmit`, and `walkietalk voice-agent-check` with `--supervised --transmit`. Ctrl+C releases the transmitter.

Do not transmit to "test" on your own. Operator `approve` is message review, not permission to key.

## Upgrade

```bash
cd walkietalk
git pull --ff-only
cargo install --locked --path crates/walkietalk
walkietalk config-check
```

Compare `crates/walkietalk/templates/config.toml` with their config after an upgrade. `config-check` reports unknown or invalid settings.

For errors, use `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` (https://github.com/bbusenius/walkietalk/blob/main/docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md).

# Walkietalk how it works

Ground every command in the public repo `bbusenius/walkietalk` on `main` (Rust). If the user's checkout disagrees, read that tree before quoting a command. Do not invent flags. The full reference is `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`.

## What it is

A Linux radio bridge. The user speaks into a walkie-talkie, says a configured wake phrase, and the bridge asks an AI agent or sends a transcribed message to a contact. Supported agents named in the README are Grok, Codex, Hermes, and Claude. WhatsApp and Signal messaging are optional.

When someone asks what walkietalk does or looks like, link the launch video: [AI on a walkie-talkie](https://youtu.be/yzKpN5zB7zA).

## Backends

STT, the text agent, and TTS are chosen independently, unless the agent backend is `grok-realtime`, which handles recognition, the agent, and the voice in one session.

From `docs/BACKENDS.md` and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`:

- Recognition `[stt] backend`: `whisper` (default), `grok`, `grok-api`
- Agent `[agent] backend`: `stub` (default), `hermes`, `codex`, `grok`, `claude`, `claude-api`, `grok-realtime`
- Voice `[tts] backend`: `piper` (default), `grok`, `grok-api`, `hermes`

Account logins stay with that CLI (`grok login`, `codex login`, `claude auth login`). Billed API keys (`XAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) are never a silent fallback. Secrets go in `credentials.toml` beside the config, not in `config.toml`.

With `grok-realtime`, audio streams to xAI while someone speaks, so unaddressed audio is uploaded before the wake check runs on the server's transcript.

## Wake

`[wake] wake_phrase` is required. Contacts use `wake_phrase` in their `[messaging.signal]` or `[messaging.whatsapp]` section. Matching compares words and ignores case and punctuation. The config that `walkietalk init` writes uses `charlotte` with aliases `charlot` and `sharlot`. The wake phrase is not a procedure word.

## PTT

The reference setup keys with serial DTR. `[ptt] line` is `dtr` (default) or `rts`, and walkietalk holds the other line low. `[ptt] port` should be a stable path such as `/dev/serial/by-id/...`.

## Transmit limits

`[radio] max_tx_seconds` is a hard limit on one transmission and defaults to 10. `settle_seconds` (0.2) is the delay between keying and audio. `post_tx_mute_seconds` (2) pauses listening after the transmitter is released. Walkietalk crops agent replies longer than the speech budget. It never crops a station ID.

## Station ID

`[radio.station_id]` has `callsign` (empty disables identification), `mode` (`off`, `end-of-reply` by default, or `interval` with `interval_seconds`, default 900), and `method` (`voice` by default, or `morse` for an 800 Hz tone at 20 words per minute). `walkietalk morse-check [CALLSIGN] --output id.wav` writes the Morse ID to a WAV and never transmits. If a due ID cannot be prepared or sent, `talk` stops with an error.

## Listening, sleep, and shutdown

- `[listening] mode` is `conversation` (default), where the wake phrase opens a follow-up window of `follow_up_seconds` (30), or `wake-phrase`, where every request starts with the wake phrase.
- `[sleep]` closes the open conversation. The config `init` writes uses the phrase "go to sleep". Remove the section to disable sleep.
- `[shutdown]` is off by default. A phrase arms it and a code confirms it within `confirm_window_seconds` (30). It only exits walkietalk. Anyone on the channel can hear the phrase, so it is a convenience, not security.

## SARNEG mode

`[sarneg] enabled = true` with a `key` of ten letters, none repeated, makes the agent, each contact, and sleep wake by their `sarneg_code` instead of their phrases. The key's letter at position d stands for digit d. Codes are at least 3 digits, written as strings so leading zeros stay. Shutdown is still armed by its plain phrase and confirmed by `shutdown.sarneg_code`. NATO phonetic words are recognized more reliably than spoken letters. One key serves every code.

## Messaging

Signal uses `signal-cli` and WhatsApp uses `wacli`. Each service has one contact in `to`. Walkietalk handles stored messages only, never live calls. `send_as_voice` sends the recording as a voice note instead of a transcript, and `transcribe_voice` reads incoming voice notes as text. Without operator mode, the open contact's messages are read whenever the radio is idle. Receive-only `talk` prints them instead.

## Operator mode

`[messaging] operator_mode = true` holds every incoming and outgoing message in one review queue. `walkietalk operator` actions are `status` (default), `read`, `edit`, `approve`, `transmit`, `deny`, and `sleep`. Run it with continuous `talk --capture`, since WAV input and `--once` are refused. `walkietalk talk --capture --transmit --panel` shows the review controls in the same terminal and needs operator mode on. Approval does not decide whether a transmission is allowed on the user's radio service, and the operator must still monitor the station while it transmits.

## Checks that never transmit

`config-check`, `check`, `devices`, `agent-check`, `tts-check`, `morse-check`, `listen`, `models`, and `talk` without `--transmit` do not key the radio. `ptt`, `play`, and `voice-agent-check --supervised` without `--transmit` simulate keying. `voice-agent-check` always calls the billed realtime API, with or without `--transmit`. A live radio needs transmit consent, which exists only with `--transmit`.

skills.name: GMRS license signup
skills.description: Use when the user wants a US GMRS license or asks what one involves. Explain that there is no exam, read the current fee and term from the FCC, and offer to fill out the FCC application for them in your browser as far as the site allows. No legal advice.
skills.content:
---
name: GMRS license signup
description: >-
  Use when the user wants a US GMRS license or asks what one involves. Explain
  that there is no exam, read the current fee and term from the FCC, and offer
  to fill out the FCC application for them in your browser as far as the site
  allows. No legal advice.
---
# GMRS license signup

Tell the user these facts up front, then offer to fill out the application for them. Start only when they say they want to. Do not give legal advice.

## What it is

- There is no exam. The GMRS rule asks only that the applicant be eligible, apply, and pay the FCC fees ([47 CFR 95.1705](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-95/subpart-E/section-95.1705)).
- Eligibility is 18 or older and not a representative of a foreign government ([FCC GMRS page](https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/general-mobile-radio-service-gmrs)).
- One license covers the licensee's immediate family members, who may operate the licensee's GMRS stations at any age. Section 95.1705(c) lists who counts as immediate family.
- The term is ten years. Renewal opens 90 days before the license expires. After it expires, they must apply for a new license.
- The fee on 2026-10-11 was $35 for a new GMRS (ZA) license, with no regulatory fee, from the FCC's [Personal Service and Amateur Application Fees](https://www.fcc.gov/personal-service-and-amateur-application-fees) page (fee guide effective May 23, 2025). Fees change. Re-read that page before you quote a fee, and quote what it says that day.

If you can't load an FCC page, say so and give the link. Do not fill the gap from memory.

## Fill it out for them

Offer to do the filing in your own browser, as much of it as the FCC site allows. The FCC screens confuse most people, so this is the main help. If they'd rather do it themselves, walk them through each screen instead.

1. **FRN in [CORES](https://apps.fcc.gov/cores).** They need an FCC Registration Number. Open CORES in your browser. Hand them the screen to create their account and choose their password, or to sign in. Then fill in the registration from the details they give you.
2. **Application in the [Universal Licensing System](https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/systems-utilities/universal-licensing-system).** Open "File Online", sign in with their FRN (hand them the screen for the password), and start a new application for radio service code ZA (GMRS). Ask for the details one screen at a time and fill each screen. Read every eligibility or certification question to them word for word and enter only the answer they give. Never answer one for them or guess.
3. **Review and submit.** Before you submit, show them a summary of every answer and get a clear yes. Submit only after that yes.
4. **Pay.** The fee is paid in CORES after the application is submitted. They enter their own payment details, or follow your purchase rules if they ask you to pay. Tell them what the FCC page shows for the amount before they pay.
5. **After.** Tell them the confirmation or file number the FCC shows, and that the grant and call sign arrive later. Save in memory that the application was filed and when, never their FRN, password, or payment details.

Do not state a form number or a processing time from memory. Read it from the FCC page you're on. If a saved link fails, go back to the ULS page and use the link the FCC shows now. If the FCC posts an outage notice for CORES or ULS, tell them and suggest trying again later.

A granted call sign belongs in that user's private config (`[radio.station_id] callsign`), not in a skill, a README example, or chat that will be shared.

description: >-

  a transmission is permitted. Read the current FCC and eCFR text and answer
  from it, with the section and link. Not legal advice. Do not block use.
---
# FCC GMRS rules

You are not a lawyer. Say that when a question is about what the user is allowed to do. Do not refuse to run walkietalk because you are unsure. The user decides.

When they ask about US GMRS, read the current text before you answer. Do not answer from memory.

- [47 CFR Part 95 Subpart E](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-95/subpart-E) is the rule text. Open it and read the sections that bear on the question.
- [FCC GMRS page](https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/general-mobile-radio-service-gmrs) is the FCC's own summary. Read it too.

Answer the question from those pages. Name the section you used (for example § 95.1751). Quote the short part that decides it. Give them the link. If the text does not cover the question, say so.

Do not stop at handing them the link. Do not limit the answer to what the walkietalk README mentions.

`[radio.station_id] callsign` is the user's granted station ID. Empty disables identification. Do not put a household call sign into this skill or into a shared config example.

For questions about relaying Signal or WhatsApp messages, read and quote §§ 95.1733(a)(8), 95.1745, and 95.1749, and the FCC page's paragraph on interconnection with other networks. The walkietalk README's IMPORTANT box takes no position. For station identification, read § 95.1751.

If they want a license, use the GMRS license signup skill. If they do not, keep going.

skills.name: Radio procedure words
skills.description: Use when the user is on the radio or asks what roger, copy, over, out, say again, stand by, wilco, breaker, a 10-code, or a Q-code means. Use the words as an operator would. Do not treat them as costume or as the wake phrase.
skills.content:
---
name: Radio procedure words
description: >-
  Use when the user is on the radio or asks what roger, copy, over, out, say
  again, stand by, wilco, breaker, a 10-code, or a Q-code means. Use the words
  as an operator would. Do not treat them as costume or as the wake phrase.
---
# Radio procedure words

Use these as an operator would. Do not role-play. The walkietalk repo does not define a procedure glossary. Its message templates sometimes end a spoken line with "over" and use "Standing by" as a sleep confirmation. Those are product phrases, not a word list.

The wake phrase is `[wake] wake_phrase` in config. It is not one of these words.

- **Roger** and **copy**: I understood that. Not "yes."
- **Wilco**: I understood and will do it. Not the same as roger.
- **Over**: I am done; your turn. Expect a reply.
- **Out**: I am done; no reply expected. Do not say "over and out."
- **Say again**: Repeat your last transmission.
- **Stand by**: Wait.
- **Go ahead**: I am listening; proceed.
- **Breaker**: CB usage, a request to join a channel. Not a GMRS requirement.

If the user asks about a 10-code or a Q-code, give that meaning in one sentence and say which service actually uses it. Do not withhold operator terms. Use a word the same way in later replies.

skills.description: Use when spelling letters on the radio, normalizing spoken letter codes, or explaining the NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet.
skills.content:
---
name: NATO phonetic alphabet
description: >-
  Use when spelling letters on the radio, normalizing spoken letter codes, or
  explaining the NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet.
---
# NATO phonetic alphabet

Use the ICAO/NATO spelling alphabet for letters on voice radio. Digits are spoken as ordinary numbers unless a local procedure says otherwise.

| Letter | Word |
| --- | --- |
| A | Alfa |
| B | Bravo |
| C | Charlie |
| D | Delta |
| E | Echo |
| F | Foxtrot |
| G | Golf |
| H | Hotel |
| I | India |
| J | Juliett |
| K | Kilo |
| L | Lima |
| M | Mike |
| N | November |
| O | Oscar |
| P | Papa |
| Q | Quebec |
| R | Romeo |
| S | Sierra |
| T | Tango |
| U | Uniform |
| V | Victor |
| W | Whiskey |
| X | X-ray |
| Y | Yankee |
| Z | Zulu |

## How to use it

- Spell a letter group one word per letter: `OHT` is "Oscar Hotel Tango".
- When normalizing speech-to-text for letter codes, treat each phonetic word as its first letter, and treat a lone letter the same way.
- Accept common misspellings of the words when matching (`Alpha` for `Alfa`, `Juliet` for `Juliett`) unless exact spelling matters.
- Prefer this alphabet over homemade words when the traffic needs to be clear.

skills.name: SARNEG field booklet
skills.description: Use when someone asks for a printable SARNEG code booklet or field book for walkietalk SARNEG mode. Make a blank, bordered, trim-to-size PDF. Never print real keys or codes in it.
skills.content:
---
name: SARNEG field booklet
description: >-
  Use when someone asks for a printable SARNEG code booklet or field book for
  walkietalk SARNEG mode. Make a blank, bordered, trim-to-size PDF. Never print
  real keys or codes in it.
---
# SARNEG field booklet

Make a blank booklet people fill in by hand so they can use walkietalk's SARNEG mode on the radio. It is printable on US Letter, and the pages are trimmed down to pocket size.

## Before building

- Get the list of codes from the current walkietalk `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`, in the `[sarneg]` section and every `sarneg_code` row. Build from public `main` (https://github.com/bbusenius/walkietalk) unless the user points at a checkout.
- As of the SARNEG-mode merge, the codes are: the agent wake (`[wake]`), each messaging contact (`[messaging.signal]`, `[messaging.whatsapp]`), sleep (`sleep.sarneg_code`), and shutdown (`shutdown.sarneg_code`). In SARNEG mode the shutdown phrase is still spoken in plain words and only its confirming code is SARNEG. There is one global key in `[sarneg] key`. If the docs differ, follow the docs.
- Never read credentials files, and never copy anyone's real key, codes, phrases, or contact names into the booklet. Every field stays blank.

## Format

- Each US Letter sheet holds four pages of 4.25 x 5.5 in, in a 2 x 2 grid, printed single-sided.
- Reading order on each sheet is top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Cut each sheet into quarters, stack in order, and staple.
- Every page, cover included, gets a solid border about 0.28 in inside its trim edge. Home printers can't reach closer than about 0.25 in to the paper edge. Add light crop marks, including a cross at the center of the sheet.
- Use big, high-contrast black-on-white type. Avoid heavy fills except the cover band. Number the inside pages.

## Pages, in order

1. Cover: "TOP SECRET" in a black band, then "SARNEG Field Book", "for walkietalk", and blank lines for Agent and Team.
2. Secret Key: one row of ten blank slots with the digits 0 to 9 centered under each, in the same row. Add a reminder box saying 10 letters, no letter used twice, and never say the key on air. Add a "Key starts on (date)" line.
3. How to Use, in four plain steps: find each digit under the key, write the letter above it, turn each letter into its radio word, then press the button and say the radio words followed by your message. Say that radio words are recognized better than plain letters. If the docs say there is a minimum code length, include it.
4. Example, labeled "Practice only. Do not use this key!" Use a valid made-up key that you did not suggest to the user as a real key. Show the number, the letters, the radio words, and a sample call. Check the encoding in code, both directions.
5. One page per code: the title, a one-line plain description, a "Number:" row of about 6 blank slots, a "Letters:" row with the same slots, and "Say it:" with 2 or 3 writing lines. The shutdown page adds a "Phrase (plain words):" line above the code.
6. Two "Other code: ____" pages with the same layout.
7. Radio Words A-M and N-Z on two pages: the full ICAO/NATO alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu).
8. Notes pages as needed to fill the last sheet, then a back cover with "TOP SECRET" and "If found, return to:" lines.

## Build and check

- Use Python with reportlab (`pip install reportlab`) on your own computer. Draw each quarter page in its own coordinates, with helpers for centered text, title rule, blank slots, writing lines, and borders.
- Assert in the script that the NATO list has 26 entries in A to Z order, that the example key has 10 unique letters, and that the example number encodes and decodes correctly.
- Render previews with `pdftoppm -r 80 -png`, open every sheet, and fix any overlap, clipped text, misaligned digits, or border too close to the edge.
- Deliver the PDF along with one or two preview images, and give short print and cut instructions.
